Sample.evidence_source: [/page/6/Text/4] Results of the satisfaction survey administered to children and parents at posttest, revealed that 100% of children and 94% of parents rated the intervention as helpful. Additionally, all of the parents indicated that they had noticed some generalization of skills. That is, their children were using the skills taught in the groups to cope with real-world problems outside of the group. All of the parents rated the family intervention as useful. Sixty percent of the parents felt the brief family intervention was adequate to their needs, but a sizable minority (40%) felt more extended family sessions would have been helpful.

IPT.evidence_source: [/page/6/Text/3] These findings are consistent with the prediction that the intervention would be successful in decreasing negative cognitive patterns and enhancing coping skills.
IPT.warning: Intervention described as decreasing negative cognitive patterns and enhancing coping skills, which is CBT-flavored, but not explicitly named IPT.

Source.evidence_source: [/page/5/Text/6] A simple repeated measures ANOVA on the CDI measures at the three time points did not yield a significant Group × Quadratic Effect, F(1, 20) = 1.7, [/page/6/Text/3] As predicted, results indicated a significant intervention effect for the ATQ Negative Thoughts Score, F(1,20) = 4.50, p < .02 and Internalizing Coping on the Self-Report Coping Scale, F(1,20) = 3.44, p < .04. Marginal effects were also found for Seeking Social Support, F(1,20) = 1.77, p < .10, and Problem Solving, F(1,20) = 1.54, p < .10, on the Self-Report Coping Scale.
